analysis.title: US retail sales and manufacturing suggest strong momentum
key_insights: October US retail sales rose 0.2% MoM versus 0.1% consensus. The control group (excludes gasoline, autos, building materials and restaurants) rose 0.6% MoM versus 0.3% expected, and September was revised up 0.4pp to 0.5% MoM.

The retail sales figures are nominal. Hotter-than-anticipated October inflation leaves headline sales negative in real terms and core activity flat to slightly higher, implying a smaller consumer contribution to 4Q GDP growth than in 3Q.

The retail strength is concentrated in the miscellaneous store category, up 4.7% MoM after a 3% fall in September. Gasoline stations and health and personal care rose 1.5% each and non-store/internet rose 1.2%. Furniture (-2.3%), autos (-1.6%), clothing (-0.7%) and sporting goods (-0.7%) fell.

Retail sales are a shrinking share of total consumer spending. Middle and lower income households face wage growth that lags the cost of living and spend more on goods. High income households, with surging wealth, account for a growing share of spending and spend more on services that retail sales exclude. ING expects non-retail spending to keep outperforming.

October industrial production fell 0.4% MoM versus +0.1% consensus, driven by a 4.3% drop in utilities output on mild weather. Mining fell 0.8%. Manufacturing rose 0.3%, with business equipment +1% and defence and space +0.9%.
Within manufacturing, motor vehicles and parts output rose 4.4% and computer and electronic products rose 1.4%. Aircraft, electrical equipment and appliances, and fabricated metal products were weak.

The October ISM manufacturing index rose to 55.5 from 54.5 in September. Manufacturing has added 101,000 jobs year-to-date after three years of consecutive declines, and average weekly hours are up 30 minutes to 40.5 versus 12 months ago.

ING attributes the manufacturing improvement to tariffs, low US energy costs (helping steel and glass), and US growth outperforming other major markets. It expects advanced manufacturing (tech, electronics, transport, power-related) to keep outperforming on strong tech investment pipelines, while labour-intensive commoditised sectors keep shrinking, since tariffs do not offset high US production costs and these producers face retaliatory tariffs abroad.

sector_views.rationale: Strong tech investment pipelines and the sector has significantly outperformed other manufacturing sectors.
Tariffs are not enough to offset high US production costs, and these producers face retaliatory tariffs in foreign markets.

risk_factors: Nominal retail sales gains are eroded by hotter October inflation, leaving headline sales negative in real terms.
Middle and lower income households are squeezed by wage growth below cost-of-living increases, and consumer sentiment readings are weak.
Traditional labour-intensive manufacturing faces foreign competition and retaliatory tariffs that tariffs on imports do not offset.
geopolitical: US tariffs and retaliatory foreign tariffs are discussed as affecting the competitiveness of US manufacturing.
US energy security is cited as a factor supporting US manufacturing.

tension_points.bull_case: Control group sales rose 0.6% MoM versus 0.3% expected with a September upward revision, and high income households with surging wealth are driving a growing share of spending.
tension_points.bear_case: The figures are nominal, so higher inflation leaves headline sales negative in real terms and core flat to slightly higher. Middle and lower income households face wages lagging the cost of living and weak sentiment.
